title: Muscle Length Testing
keywords: muscle length tightness tight muscles flexibility stretch thomas ober ely slr popliteal angle gastrocnemius soleus lunge
summary: Test 14 key muscles for length — Thomas, Ely, Ober, SLR, 90/90, calf, adductors, pectorals, lats and neck — with correct stabilisation, normal values and how to tell muscle from joint or nerve.
ur: 14 ahem muscles ki length test karna — Thomas, Ely, Ober, SLR, 90/90, calf, pectorals aur neck — sahi stabilisation aur normal values ke saath.

sources.title: Kendall et al. — Muscles: Testing and Function with Posture and Pain (5th ed.)
Norkin & White — Measurement of Joint Motion (5th ed.)
Bennell et al. (1998) — weight-bearing lunge test reliability

goals.beginner: Know which test checks which muscle and how the patient lies.
goals.intermediate: Perform each test with the right stabilisation and know the normal result.
goals.advanced: Spot compensations and read a positive test correctly.
goals.expert: Tell muscle from joint or nerve, and turn findings into treatment.

atlas.title: Modified Thomas test
atlas.subtitle: Hip flexors — iliopsoas (one-joint) and rectus femoris (two-joint)
atlas.tip: Flatten the back first — the lumbar spine is the commonest place to hide hip-flexor tightness.

fields.label: Muscle(s)
fields.value: Hip flexors — iliopsoas (one-joint) and rectus femoris (two-joint)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting at the very end of the plinth, then rolled back to supine holding the untested knee to the chest

fields.label: Procedure
fields.value: Hold the opposite knee just enough to flatten the lumbar spine, then let the test leg hang relaxed over the end of the plinth

fields.label: Normal finding
fields.value: Back of the thigh rests on the plinth (hip 0°), knee flexed about 80–90°, thigh in neutral

fields.label: Tight (positive) finding
fields.value: Thigh stays above the plinth (iliopsoas); knee flexed less than 80° (rectus femoris); thigh drifts outward (TFL/ITB)

fields.label: Errors & compensations
fields.value: Pulling the opposite knee too far (excess posterior tilt exaggerates tightness) or too little (lumbar extension hides it)
fields.ask: Common error or compensation in the {title}?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: If the raised thigh drops to the plinth when you passively extend the knee, the limit was rectus femoris (two-joint), not iliopsoas.

fields.label: Muscle(s)
fields.value: Rectus femoris

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Prone, hips in neutral, pelvis flat on the plinth

fields.label: Procedure
fields.value: Passively bend the knee, bringing the heel towards the buttock, while watching the pelvis and hip

fields.label: Normal finding
fields.value: Heel reaches (or nearly reaches) the buttock with the pelvis staying flat

fields.label: Tight (positive) finding
fields.value: The buttock rises — the hip flexes on the same side as the knee bends

fields.label: Errors & compensations
fields.value: Watching the knee angle only and missing the hip flexing or the low back arching
fields.ask: Common error or compensation in the {title}?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: The prone knee bend also tensions the femoral nerve (L2–L4): anterior-thigh paraesthesia suggests neural sensitivity rather than muscle length.

atlas.title: Ober test
atlas.subtitle: Iliotibial band and tensor fasciae latae

fields.label: Muscle(s)
fields.value: Iliotibial band and tensor fasciae latae

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Side-lying on the untested side, lower hip and knee bent for stability

fields.label: Procedure
fields.value: Stabilise the pelvis, abduct and slightly extend the top hip (knee bent 90°, or straight in the modified test), then let it lower

fields.label: Normal finding
fields.value: Thigh drops below horizontal (adducts about 10° past neutral)

fields.label: Tight (positive) finding
fields.value: Thigh stays abducted above horizontal

fields.label: Errors & compensations
fields.value: Letting the hip flex or internally rotate, or the pelvis roll back — a false negative
fields.ask: Common error or compensation in the {title}?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: The modified Ober (knee straight) spares the patellofemoral joint and femoral nerve. Stretching the ITB itself changes little — target TFL and gluteal tissues.

fields.label: Muscle(s)
fields.value: Hamstrings (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine, opposite leg flat on the plinth, pelvis neutral

fields.label: Procedure
fields.value: Lift the straight leg (knee fully extended, ankle relaxed) until firm resistance or the pelvis starts to tilt; measure hip flexion

fields.label: Normal finding
fields.value: About 80° of hip flexion or more

fields.label: Tight (positive) finding
fields.value: Hip flexion below about 70° with a stretch felt in the back of the thigh

fields.label: Errors & compensations
fields.value: Letting the knee bend, the opposite thigh lift or the pelvis rotate
fields.ask: Common error or compensation in the {title}?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: If symptoms change when you add ankle dorsiflexion or neck flexion (sensitising), the limit is neural — not hamstring length.

fields.label: Muscle(s)
fields.value: Hamstrings (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine, hip held at 90° flexion (thigh vertical), opposite leg flat

fields.label: Procedure
fields.value: Keep the thigh vertical and extend the knee until resistance; measure how far it stays short of full extension

fields.label: Normal finding
fields.value: Knee extends to within about 20° of full extension

fields.label: Tight (positive) finding
fields.value: Knee stays more than 20° short of full extension (popliteal angle over 20°)

fields.label: Errors & compensations
fields.value: Letting the hip drift out of 90° or the opposite leg lift
fields.ask: Common error or compensation in the {title}?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Holding the hip at 90° stops the pelvis tilting, so it isolates hamstring length better than the SLR — and it is quick to re-test after treatment.

fields.label: Muscle(s)
fields.value: Gastrocnemius (two-joint calf muscle)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine or long sitting, knee fully extended, subtalar joint neutral

fields.label: Procedure
fields.value: Dorsiflex the ankle with the knee straight and the subtalar joint neutral; measure with a goniometer

fields.label: Normal finding
fields.value: At least 10° of dorsiflexion with the knee straight

fields.label: Tight (positive) finding
fields.value: Less than 10° dorsiflexion with the knee straight, improving when the knee bends

fields.label: Errors & compensations
fields.value: Letting the foot pronate (midfoot motion looks like dorsiflexion) or the knee bend
fields.ask: Common error or compensation in the {title}?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Re-test with the knee bent: a big gain means gastrocnemius is the limit; little gain points to soleus or the ankle joint.

fields.label: Muscle(s)
fields.value: Soleus (one-joint calf muscle)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Prone with the knee bent to 90° (or the weight-bearing lunge)

fields.label: Procedure
fields.value: With the knee bent 90° to slacken gastrocnemius, dorsiflex the ankle with the subtalar joint neutral and measure

fields.label: Normal finding
fields.value: About 20° of dorsiflexion with the knee bent

fields.label: Tight (positive) finding
fields.value: Less than about 20° dorsiflexion with the knee bent and a firm, muscular end-feel

fields.label: Errors & compensations
fields.value: Pronating the foot, or measuring with the knee straight
fields.ask: Common error or compensation in the {title}?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: A hard end-feel suggests the talocrural joint (e.g. anterior impingement) rather than soleus — mobilise the joint instead of stretching.

fields.label: Muscle(s)
fields.value: Hip adductors (one-joint) and gracilis (two-joint)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine, pelvis level and stabilised, legs straight

fields.label: Procedure
fields.value: Abduct the straight leg until the pelvis starts to move; repeat with the knee bent to separate gracilis

fields.label: Normal finding
fields.value: About 40–45° of abduction with the knee straight

fields.label: Tight (positive) finding
fields.value: Less than about 40° abduction; more range with the knee bent points to gracilis

fields.label: Errors & compensations
fields.value: Letting the pelvis tilt sideways or the opposite leg follow
fields.ask: Common error or compensation in the {title}?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Relevant in groin pain (pair it with the adductor squeeze test) and in spastic adductors after UMN lesions (scissoring gait).

fields.label: Muscle(s)
fields.value: Piriformis (deep hip external rotator)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine, hip bent to about 60° with the foot beside the opposite knee

fields.label: Procedure
fields.value: Stabilise the pelvis and draw the bent hip across the body into adduction (adding internal rotation); compare sides

fields.label: Normal finding
fields.value: Knee reaches roughly to the midline without deep buttock pain, equal to the other side

fields.label: Tight (positive) finding
fields.value: Restricted adduction with deep buttock tightness or reproduced buttock pain

fields.label: Errors & compensations
fields.value: Letting the pelvis lift off the plinth or the lumbar spine rotate
fields.ask: Common error or compensation in the {title}?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Beyond about 90° of hip flexion piriformis becomes an internal rotator, so stretch it in external rotation in deep flexion (figure-4). Screen the lumbar spine and sciatic nerve first.

fields.label: Muscle(s)
fields.value: Pectoralis major (sternal and clavicular parts)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine hooklying with the lumbar spine flat

fields.label: Procedure
fields.value: Place the straight arm in about 90° abduction (clavicular part) and 135° abduction (sternal part) and let it lower towards the plinth

fields.label: Normal finding
fields.value: The arm rests on the plinth in both positions

fields.label: Tight (positive) finding
fields.value: Arm stays above the plinth — at 90° the clavicular part, at 135° the sternal part

fields.label: Errors & compensations
fields.value: Letting the lumbar spine arch or the trunk rotate
fields.ask: Common error or compensation in the {title}?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Often short with rounded-shoulder (upper-crossed) posture; pair stretching with thoracic extension and lower-trapezius strengthening.

fields.label: Muscle(s)
fields.value: Pectoralis minor

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine, arms by the sides, knees bent

fields.label: Procedure
fields.value: With the patient relaxed, measure from the back of the acromion to the plinth and compare sides

fields.label: Normal finding
fields.value: Back of the shoulder rests near the plinth (acromion about 2.5 cm or less from the table)

fields.label: Tight (positive) finding
fields.value: Acromion held well above the plinth (more than about 2.5 cm), shoulder protracted

fields.label: Errors & compensations
fields.value: Letting the patient actively retract or shrug the shoulder; not comparing sides
fields.ask: Common error or compensation in the {title}?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: A short pectoralis minor tilts the scapula anteriorly and narrows the subacromial space — relevant in shoulder impingement.

fields.label: Muscle(s)
fields.value: Latissimus dorsi (and teres major)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine hooklying, lumbar spine flat on the plinth

fields.label: Procedure
fields.value: Raise both straight arms overhead, close to the head, keeping the low back flat

fields.label: Normal finding
fields.value: Arms reach the plinth overhead (about 180°) with the lumbar spine flat

fields.label: Tight (positive) finding
fields.value: Arms cannot reach the plinth, or the low back arches to get them there

fields.label: Errors & compensations
fields.value: Letting the lumbar spine extend or the elbows bend
fields.ask: Common error or compensation in the {title}?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Limits overhead reach in swimmers and lifters and drives compensatory lumbar extension; re-test with the arms externally rotated.

fields.label: Muscle(s)
fields.value: Upper trapezius

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting or supine, shoulder depressed and stabilised

fields.label: Procedure
fields.value: Hold the shoulder down, then side-flex the neck away, flex it slightly and rotate it towards the tested side

fields.label: Normal finding
fields.value: About 45° side flexion with a soft stretch, equal both sides

fields.label: Tight (positive) finding
fields.value: Reduced side flexion with a firm pull along the top of the shoulder

fields.label: Errors & compensations
fields.value: Letting the shoulder elevate or rotating the head the wrong way
fields.ask: Common error or compensation in the {title}?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Upper trapezius turns the head to the opposite side, so it is stretched by turning towards the same side. Check for cervical joint signs before calling it 'tight'.

fields.label: Muscle(s)
fields.value: Levator scapulae

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting, shoulder depressed and stabilised

fields.label: Procedure
fields.value: Flex the neck, side-flex and rotate it away from the tested side (nose towards the opposite armpit)

fields.label: Normal finding
fields.value: Nose reaches towards the opposite armpit with a soft stretch, equal both sides

fields.label: Tight (positive) finding
fields.value: Restricted motion with a pull at the superior angle of the scapula

fields.label: Errors & compensations
fields.value: Letting the scapula elevate; forcing end range in an irritable neck
fields.ask: Common error or compensation in the {title}?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Levator scapulae turns the head to the same side, so it is stretched by turning away — the opposite of upper trapezius.

concepts.title: What a muscle length test is
concepts.body: A length test **passively elongates a muscle across every joint it crosses** and checks whether it reaches normal range. You compare with the norm **and the other side**. A short muscle limits motion in one direction and often pulls the body into a posture.
bullets: Tight (short) = less range than normal, with a firm muscular stop
Weak ≠ short — test strength separately with MMT
concepts.ur: Muscle ko us ke saare joints par passively stretch karke dekhte hain ke normal length tak pohanchta hai ya nahi — aur dono sides compare karte hain.

concepts.title: One-joint vs two-joint muscles
concepts.body: A **two-joint muscle** is only fully stretched when **both** joints are positioned. Change the second joint to tell muscles apart.

concepts.title: Where to stop
concepts.body: Stop at the **first firm resistance** or the **first compensation** — the pelvis tilting, the spine arching or the opposite leg lifting. Range gained after a compensation belongs to another joint.

concepts.title: Stabilise the proximal attachment
concepts.body: Most errors come from letting the proximal segment move. Fix it, and watch it.

head: Test
Watch for
rows: Lumbar spine lifting (too little hug) or flattening too much
Pelvis tilting posteriorly, opposite thigh lifting
Hip flexing/internally rotating, pelvis rolling back
Foot pronating — midfoot motion mimics dorsiflexion

concepts.title: The weight-bearing lunge (knee-to-wall) test
concepts.body: Facing a wall, the patient lunges the knee to touch the wall with the heel down. Move the foot back until the knee only just touches. A **toe-to-wall distance of about 9–10 cm or more** (tibial inclination about 35°+) is usually normal; a **side difference over about 2 cm** is meaningful. It is reliable and reflects functional dorsiflexion (soleus + ankle joint).

concepts.title: Muscle, joint or nerve?
concepts.body: **Structural differentiation** changes a distant body part that moves the nerve but not the muscle. If symptoms change, the nerve is involved.
bullets: SLR: add ankle dorsiflexion or neck flexion — hamstrings don't change, the sciatic nerve does
Prone knee bend: add neck flexion (slump side-lying) for the femoral nerve
Calf: a hard, abrupt end-feel suggests the ankle joint, not the muscle

concepts.title: End-feel tells the story
concepts.body: A short muscle gives a **firm, slightly elastic** end-feel with a stretch felt in the muscle. **Hard** = bone or joint block. **Spasm** (sudden guarding) = irritability or protection. **Empty** (pain stops you before resistance) = think serious pathology.

concepts.title: Tight, guarded or hypermobile?
concepts.body: Reduced range can be true shortening, **protective guarding** (it relaxes with reassurance or hold-relax) or **neural sensitivity**. And some patients are **hypermobile** — screen with the Beighton score (≥5/9 in adults suggests generalised hypermobility) before stretching anyone.

concepts.title: From finding to treatment
concepts.body: Treat a short muscle only if it matters to the problem. Static stretching **15–30 s × 2–4 repetitions, most days, for at least 6 weeks** changes range; strengthen the lengthened antagonist; and **re-test with the same test** to prove change.
bullets: Short hip flexors + weak glutes → stretch + glute strengthening
Short pectoralis minor + shoulder pain → stretch + lower-trapezius/serratus work
Spasticity is not shortness — manage tone first (see Tone & Coordination)

questions.prompt: A muscle length test is performed…
options: Only with the patient standing
Actively against resistance
Passively, elongating the muscle across the joints it crosses
Only after warming up for 20 minutes
questions.explain: Length = passive elongation; strength is tested with MMT.

questions.prompt: To fully stretch the hamstrings you need…
options: Hip extension with the knee flexed
Hip flexion with the knee flexed
Hip abduction with the knee flexed
Hip flexion with the knee extended
questions.explain: Two-joint muscle: hip flexion + knee extension.

questions.prompt: Why compare both sides?
options: Normal values vary; asymmetry is often more meaningful than the number
To warm the muscle up
Only the right side has norms
It's faster
questions.explain: The other side is the patient's own normal.

questions.prompt: Which test checks the iliotibial band/TFL?
options: Thomas test
Ober test
SLR
Ely's test
questions.explain: Ober = ITB/TFL in side-lying.

questions.prompt: In the Thomas test, the opposite knee is held to the chest to…
options: Relax the abdominals
Flatten the lumbar spine and fix the pelvis
Stretch the hamstrings
Test hip flexor strength
questions.explain: It removes lumbar lordosis so hip-flexor tightness can show.

questions.prompt: Gastrocnemius length is tested with the knee…
options: Extended
Flexed to 45°
In any position
Flexed to 90°
questions.explain: Knee straight puts the two-joint gastrocnemius on stretch.

questions.prompt: Soleus length is tested with the knee bent because…
options: It stretches the soleus more at the knee
It is more comfortable
It tests the hamstrings at the same time
Bending the knee slackens gastrocnemius
questions.explain: Soleus is one-joint; gastrocnemius crosses the knee.

questions.prompt: In the weight-bearing lunge test, a toe-to-wall distance of about … is usually normal.
options: 9–10 cm or more
Under 5 cm
2 cm
30 cm
questions.explain: ≈ 9–10 cm or more; side differences over ~2 cm matter.

questions.prompt: Thomas test: the thigh is raised, but drops to the plinth when you straighten the knee. Which muscle is short?
options: Sartorius
Rectus femoris
Iliopsoas
TFL
questions.explain: Releasing the knee slackens the two-joint rectus femoris.

questions.prompt: During a hamstring SLR the pelvis starts to tilt posteriorly at 60°. You should…
options: Record 60° — the range after that is lumbar/pelvic motion
Bend the knee to finish
Stop testing hamstrings altogether
Keep lifting to 90° and record 90°
questions.explain: The first compensation marks the end of muscle length.

questions.prompt: Ober test: the hip flexes as the thigh lowers. The result is…
options: Normal
A sign of hamstring tightness
Positive for ITB tightness
Unreliable — likely a false negative
questions.explain: Hip flexion lets the ITB slacken, so the thigh drops falsely.

questions.prompt: A hard, abrupt stop to ankle dorsiflexion with anterior ankle pain suggests…
options: Short soleus
Short gastrocnemius
A joint limitation (e.g. anterior impingement) rather than calf tightness
Normal end-feel
questions.explain: Muscle end-feel is firm and elastic, not hard.

questions.case: SLR stops at 50° with posterior-thigh pain. Adding ankle dorsiflexion increases the pain; neck flexion also changes it.
questions.prompt: Interpretation?
options: Short hamstrings only
Normal SLR
Neural mechanosensitivity (sciatic nerve) is limiting, not hamstring length
Hip joint OA
questions.explain: Distant sensitising movements change symptoms only when the nerve is involved.

questions.case: A runner: dorsiflexion 4° with the knee straight and 22° with the knee bent.
questions.prompt: Which structure limits dorsiflexion?
options: Talocrural joint
Tibialis anterior
Gastrocnemius
Soleus
questions.explain: Normal with the knee bent; limited only with the knee straight = gastrocnemius.

questions.case: A 19-year-old dancer has 110° SLR, elbows that hyperextend 15° and can place her palms flat on the floor.
questions.prompt: Best action before prescribing stretches?
options: Stretch the hamstrings daily
Record a positive SLR
Refer for surgery
Screen for generalised hypermobility (Beighton) — she may need control and strength, not stretching
questions.explain: Excess range is a different problem; stretching a hypermobile patient adds little.

questions.case: Thomas test: thigh 15° above the plinth, knee bent 85°, and the thigh does not drop when you extend the knee.
questions.prompt: Which muscle is short?
options: Iliopsoas (one-joint hip flexor)
Rectus femoris
TFL
Hamstrings
questions.explain: Knee position doesn't change it, so the one-joint hip flexor is the limit.

questions.case: After a stroke the elbow flexors catch at 70° on fast stretch but reach full range slowly.
questions.prompt: Is this muscle shortness?
options: Yes — short biceps
It's a joint block
No — it is velocity-dependent spasticity; slow passive range is full
Yes — short brachialis
questions.explain: Length tests are slow and passive; a speed-dependent catch is tone.

questions.case: Shoulder impingement; resting acromion 5 cm above the plinth on the painful side, 2 cm on the other.
questions.prompt: Which finding and treatment fit best?
options: Long pectoralis minor — strengthen it
Normal — no action
Short pectoralis minor — stretch it and strengthen lower trapezius/serratus anterior
Short latissimus dorsi — overhead stretching only
questions.explain: Asymmetric, raised acromion = short pectoralis minor; pair stretching with scapular control.

questions.prompt: A 'tight' muscle relaxes and gains 20° after reassurance and a hold–relax contraction. This suggests…
options: Spasticity
Hypermobility
A severe contracture
Protective guarding rather than true shortening
questions.explain: True shortening does not change within seconds.

questions.prompt: Stretching that reliably increases muscle length usually involves…
options: Ballistic bouncing only
One 5-second hold a week
15–30 s holds, 2–4 reps, most days for at least 6 weeks
Stretching only before sport
questions.explain: Range gains need regular, sustained stretching over weeks.

questions.case: Lateral knee pain in a cyclist: Ober positive; Thomas shows the thigh drifting into abduction.
questions.prompt: Treatment focus?
options: Rest only
TFL/gluteal soft tissue and hip abductor control — the ITB itself barely stretches
Aggressive ITB stretching to lengthen the band
Hamstring stretching
questions.explain: The ITB is very stiff; work on the muscles that tension it and on hip control.

questions.prompt: The 90/90 test is often preferred to the SLR for hamstrings because…
options: It needs no goniometer
It also tests the quadriceps
It tests the sciatic nerve better
Holding the hip at 90° stops pelvic tilt contaminating the result
questions.explain: Better pelvic control = purer hamstring measure.

questions.prompt: Which muscle(s) does the Modified Thomas test assess?
options: Latissimus dorsi (and teres major)
Piriformis (deep hip external rotator)
Hip flexors — iliopsoas (one-joint) and rectus femoris (two-joint)
Levator scapulae
questions.explain: Modified Thomas test: muscle(s) — Hip flexors — iliopsoas (one-joint) and rectus femoris (two-joint). Flatten the back first — the lumbar spine is the commonest place to hide hip-flexor tightness.

questions.prompt: Patient position for the Modified Thomas test?
options: Sitting at the very end of the plinth, then rolled back to supine holding the untested knee to the chest
Supine, opposite leg flat on the plinth, pelvis neutral
Supine, pelvis level and stabilised, legs straight
Prone, hips in neutral, pelvis flat on the plinth
questions.explain: Modified Thomas test: position — Sitting at the very end of the plinth, then rolled back to supine holding the untested knee to the chest. Flatten the back first — the lumbar spine is the commonest place to hide hip-flexor tightness.

questions.prompt: How is the Modified Thomas test performed?
options: Hold the opposite knee just enough to flatten the lumbar spine, then let the test leg hang relaxed over the end of the plinth
Lift the straight leg (knee fully extended, ankle relaxed) until firm resistance or the pelvis starts to tilt; measure hip flexion
Stabilise the pelvis and draw the bent hip across the body into adduction (adding internal rotation); compare sides
Abduct the straight leg until the pelvis starts to move; repeat with the knee bent to separate gracilis
questions.explain: Modified Thomas test: procedure — Hold the opposite knee just enough to flatten the lumbar spine, then let the test leg hang relaxed over the end of the plinth. Flatten the back first — the lumbar spine is the commonest place to hide hip-flexor tightness.

questions.prompt: Normal (negative) finding in the Modified Thomas test?
options: Back of the thigh rests on the plinth (hip 0°), knee flexed about 80–90°, thigh in neutral
Back of the shoulder rests near the plinth (acromion about 2.5 cm or less from the table)
The arm rests on the plinth in both positions
Arms reach the plinth overhead (about 180°) with the lumbar spine flat
questions.explain: Modified Thomas test: normal finding — Back of the thigh rests on the plinth (hip 0°), knee flexed about 80–90°, thigh in neutral. Flatten the back first — the lumbar spine is the commonest place to hide hip-flexor tightness.

questions.prompt: What shows tightness in the Modified Thomas test?
options: Arms cannot reach the plinth, or the low back arches to get them there
Hip flexion below about 70° with a stretch felt in the back of the thigh
Arm stays above the plinth — at 90° the clavicular part, at 135° the sternal part
Thigh stays above the plinth (iliopsoas); knee flexed less than 80° (rectus femoris); thigh drifts outward (TFL/ITB)
questions.explain: Modified Thomas test: tight (positive) finding — Thigh stays above the plinth (iliopsoas); knee flexed less than 80° (rectus femoris); thigh drifts outward (TFL/ITB). Flatten the back first — the lumbar spine is the commonest place to hide hip-flexor tightness.

questions.prompt: Common error or compensation in the Modified Thomas test?
options: Pulling the opposite knee too far (excess posterior tilt exaggerates tightness) or too little (lumbar extension hides it)
Watching the knee angle only and missing the hip flexing or the low back arching
Letting the hip flex or internally rotate, or the pelvis roll back — a false negative
Letting the lumbar spine arch or the trunk rotate
questions.explain: Modified Thomas test: errors & compensations — Pulling the opposite knee too far (excess posterior tilt exaggerates tightness) or too little (lumbar extension hides it). Flatten the back first — the lumbar spine is the commonest place to hide hip-flexor tightness.

questions.prompt: Which muscle(s) does the Ely's test (prone knee bend) assess?
options: Rectus femoris
Hamstrings (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris)
Piriformis (deep hip external rotator)
Upper trapezius
questions.explain: Ely's test (prone knee bend): muscle(s) — Rectus femoris.

questions.prompt: Patient position for the Ely's test (prone knee bend)?
options: Prone, hips in neutral, pelvis flat on the plinth
Supine or long sitting, knee fully extended, subtalar joint neutral
Sitting at the very end of the plinth, then rolled back to supine holding the untested knee to the chest
Side-lying on the untested side, lower hip and knee bent for stability
questions.explain: Ely's test (prone knee bend): position — Prone, hips in neutral, pelvis flat on the plinth.

questions.prompt: How is the Ely's test (prone knee bend) performed?
options: Lift the straight leg (knee fully extended, ankle relaxed) until firm resistance or the pelvis starts to tilt; measure hip flexion
Hold the opposite knee just enough to flatten the lumbar spine, then let the test leg hang relaxed over the end of the plinth
Passively bend the knee, bringing the heel towards the buttock, while watching the pelvis and hip
Abduct the straight leg until the pelvis starts to move; repeat with the knee bent to separate gracilis
questions.explain: Ely's test (prone knee bend): procedure — Passively bend the knee, bringing the heel towards the buttock, while watching the pelvis and hip.

cards.front: A muscle length test is performed…
cards.back: Passively, elongating the muscle across the joints it crosses. Length = passive elongation; strength is tested with MMT.

cards.front: To fully stretch the hamstrings you need…
cards.back: Hip flexion with the knee extended. Two-joint muscle: hip flexion + knee extension.

cards.front: Why compare both sides?
cards.back: Normal values vary; asymmetry is often more meaningful than the number. The other side is the patient's own normal.

cards.front: Which test checks the iliotibial band/TFL?
cards.back: Ober test. Ober = ITB/TFL in side-lying.

cards.front: In the Thomas test, the opposite knee is held to the chest to…
cards.back: Flatten the lumbar spine and fix the pelvis. It removes lumbar lordosis so hip-flexor tightness can show.

cards.front: Gastrocnemius length is tested with the knee…
cards.back: Extended. Knee straight puts the two-joint gastrocnemius on stretch.

cards.front: Soleus length is tested with the knee bent because…
cards.back: Bending the knee slackens gastrocnemius. Soleus is one-joint; gastrocnemius crosses the knee.

cards.front: In the weight-bearing lunge test, a toe-to-wall distance of about … is usually normal.
cards.back: 9–10 cm or more. ≈ 9–10 cm or more; side differences over ~2 cm matter.

cards.front: Thomas test: the thigh is raised, but drops to the plinth when you straighten the knee. Which muscle is short?
cards.back: Rectus femoris. Releasing the knee slackens the two-joint rectus femoris.

cards.front: During a hamstring SLR the pelvis starts to tilt posteriorly at 60°. You should…
cards.back: Record 60° — the range after that is lumbar/pelvic motion. The first compensation marks the end of muscle length.

cards.front: Ober test: the hip flexes as the thigh lowers. The result is…
cards.back: Unreliable — likely a false negative. Hip flexion lets the ITB slacken, so the thigh drops falsely.

cards.front: A hard, abrupt stop to ankle dorsiflexion with anterior ankle pain suggests…
cards.back: A joint limitation (e.g. anterior impingement) rather than calf tightness. Muscle end-feel is firm and elastic, not hard.

cards.front: SLR stops at 50° with posterior-thigh pain. Adding ankle dorsiflexion increases the pain; neck flexion also changes it. — Interpretation?
cards.back: Neural mechanosensitivity (sciatic nerve) is limiting, not hamstring length. Distant sensitising movements change symptoms only when the nerve is involved.

cards.front: A runner: dorsiflexion 4° with the knee straight and 22° with the knee bent. — Which structure limits dorsiflexion?
cards.back: Gastrocnemius. Normal with the knee bent; limited only with the knee straight = gastrocnemius.

cards.front: A 19-year-old dancer has 110° SLR, elbows that hyperextend 15° and can place her palms flat on the floor. — Best action before prescribing stretches?
cards.back: Screen for generalised hypermobility (Beighton) — she may need control and strength, not stretching. Excess range is a different problem; stretching a hypermobile patient adds little.

cards.front: Thomas test: thigh 15° above the plinth, knee bent 85°, and the thigh does not drop when you extend the knee. — Which muscle is short?
cards.back: Iliopsoas (one-joint hip flexor). Knee position doesn't change it, so the one-joint hip flexor is the limit.

cards.front: After a stroke the elbow flexors catch at 70° on fast stretch but reach full range slowly. — Is this muscle shortness?
cards.back: No — it is velocity-dependent spasticity; slow passive range is full. Length tests are slow and passive; a speed-dependent catch is tone.

cards.front: Shoulder impingement; resting acromion 5 cm above the plinth on the painful side, 2 cm on the other. — Which finding and treatment fit best?
cards.back: Short pectoralis minor — stretch it and strengthen lower trapezius/serratus anterior. Asymmetric, raised acromion = short pectoralis minor; pair stretching with scapular control.

cards.front: A 'tight' muscle relaxes and gains 20° after reassurance and a hold–relax contraction. This suggests…
cards.back: Protective guarding rather than true shortening. True shortening does not change within seconds.

cards.front: Stretching that reliably increases muscle length usually involves…
cards.back: 15–30 s holds, 2–4 reps, most days for at least 6 weeks. Range gains need regular, sustained stretching over weeks.

cards.front: Lateral knee pain in a cyclist: Ober positive; Thomas shows the thigh drifting into abduction. — Treatment focus?
cards.back: TFL/gluteal soft tissue and hip abductor control — the ITB itself barely stretches. The ITB is very stiff; work on the muscles that tension it and on hip control.

cards.front: The 90/90 test is often preferred to the SLR for hamstrings because…
cards.back: Holding the hip at 90° stops pelvic tilt contaminating the result. Better pelvic control = purer hamstring measure.

cards.front: Modified Thomas test — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: If the raised thigh drops to the plinth when you passively extend the knee, the limit was rectus femoris (two-joint), not iliopsoas.

cards.front: Ely's test (prone knee bend) — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: The prone knee bend also tensions the femoral nerve (L2–L4): anterior-thigh paraesthesia suggests neural sensitivity rather than muscle length.

cards.front: Ober test — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: The modified Ober (knee straight) spares the patellofemoral joint and femoral nerve. Stretching the ITB itself changes little — target TFL and gluteal tissues.

cards.front: Passive straight-leg raise (hamstring length) — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: If symptoms change when you add ankle dorsiflexion or neck flexion (sensitising), the limit is neural — not hamstring length.

cards.front: 90/90 active knee extension (popliteal angle) — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Holding the hip at 90° stops the pelvis tilting, so it isolates hamstring length better than the SLR — and it is quick to re-test after treatment.

cards.front: Gastrocnemius length — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Re-test with the knee bent: a big gain means gastrocnemius is the limit; little gain points to soleus or the ankle joint.

cards.front: Soleus length — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: A hard end-feel suggests the talocrural joint (e.g. anterior impingement) rather than soleus — mobilise the joint instead of stretching.

cards.front: Hip adductor length — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Relevant in groin pain (pair it with the adductor squeeze test) and in spastic adductors after UMN lesions (scissoring gait).

cards.front: Piriformis length — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Beyond about 90° of hip flexion piriformis becomes an internal rotator, so stretch it in external rotation in deep flexion (figure-4). Screen the lumbar spine and sciatic nerve first.

cards.front: Pectoralis major length — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Often short with rounded-shoulder (upper-crossed) posture; pair stretching with thoracic extension and lower-trapezius strengthening.

cards.front: Pectoralis minor length — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: A short pectoralis minor tilts the scapula anteriorly and narrows the subacromial space — relevant in shoulder impingement.

cards.front: Latissimus dorsi length — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Limits overhead reach in swimmers and lifters and drives compensatory lumbar extension; re-test with the arms externally rotated.

cards.front: Upper trapezius length — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Upper trapezius turns the head to the opposite side, so it is stretched by turning towards the same side. Check for cervical joint signs before calling it 'tight'.

cards.front: Levator scapulae length — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Levator scapulae turns the head to the same side, so it is stretched by turning away — the opposite of upper trapezius.
